claims.claim: A GFP-tagged Gbb was uniformly distributed along the apical/basal axis when expressed in ECs.
claims.source: Although a GFP-tagged Gbb (Gbb-GFP) was uniformly distributed along the apical/basal axis when expressed in ECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,A′), coexpression of Dpp redistributed Gbb-GFP toward the basal side (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C′), suggesting that Dpp and Gbb may physically interact, a notion confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C′ show Gbb-GFP redistribution with Dpp coexpression; Figure 8—figure supplement 2 shows co-IP of Dpp and Gbb.

claims.claim: vkg trans-heterozygous midguts contained an excessive number of Dl+ cells and greatly reduced number of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that vkg trans-heterozygous midguts (vkgk00236/vkg01209 and vkgk00236/vkg197) contained an excessive number of Dl+ cells and greatly reduced number of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells (Figure 8F–H), suggesting that compromised Vkg activity promotes ISC self-renewal.
claims.evidence: Figure 8F-H show increased Dl+ and decreased Su(H)-lacZ+ cells in vkg mutants.

claims.claim: vkg mutant guts contained clusters of precursor cells exhibiting high levels of BMP signaling activity.
claims.source: pMad staining revealed that vkg mutant guts contained clusters of precursor cells exhibiting high levels of BMP signaling activity (compare Figure 8J with Figure 8I, Figure 8—figure supplement 3), suggesting that Vkg regulates ISC self-renewal through restricting BMP signaling.
claims.evidence: Figure 8I-J and Figure 8—figure supplement 3 show elevated pMad in vkg mutant precursor clusters.

claims.claim: Reducing the dose of Dpp suppressed ectopic ISC formation in vkg mutant guts.
claims.source: As a further support, we found that reducing the dose of Dpp suppressed ectopic ISC formation in vkg mutant guts (Figure 8K–M).
claims.evidence: Figure 8K-M show genetic interaction between vkg and dpp.

claims.claim: vkg mutant guts retained less Dpp-GFP at the BM compared with control guts.
claims.source: In addition, we found that vkg mutant guts retained less Dpp-GFP at the BM compared with control guts (Figure 8N–Q, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 8N-Q and Figure 8—figure supplement 4 show reduced Dpp-GFP at BM in vkg mutants.

claims.claim: The BM in Drosophila midguts serves as an integral part of the ISC niche by regulating the extracellular distribution of the niche signal.
claims.source: Hence, the BM in Drosophila midguts serves as an integral part of the ISC niche by regulating the extracellular distribution of the niche signal.
claims.evidence: Concluded from vkg mutant analysis showing altered BMP distribution and ISC phenotypes.

claims.claim: BMP signaling regulates copper cell differentiation in the middle region of midguts.
claims.source: Several recent studies revealed that BMP signaling plays several roles in Drosophila adult midgut homeostasis (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013a, 2013b). First, peak levels of BMP signaling in the middle region of midguts specify copper cell differentiation (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: Cited from Guo et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2013a.

claims.claim: BMP signaling regulates ISC proliferation because reduction in BMP pathway activity results in ISC overproliferation.
claims.source: Second, BMP signaling also regulates ISC proliferation because reduction in BMP pathway activity results in ISC overproliferation (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013b), which is in line with a growth inhibitory role of BMP signaling in mammalian intestines (Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Cited from Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013b; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Both tkv8 and mad1–2 mutant clones caused excessive proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs.
claims.source: The observations that both tkv8 and mad1–2 mutant clones caused excessive proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C) and that inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated ISC proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–E) clearly support a non-cell autonomous role of BMP signaling.
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-E show non-cell autonomous effects.

claims.claim: Inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated the production of JAK-STAT and EGFR pathway ligands that fuel ISC proliferation.
claims.source: Indeed, inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated the production of JAK-STAT and EGFR pathway ligands that fuel ISC proliferation (Li et al., 2013b) (our own unpublished observation).
claims.evidence: Cited from Li et al., 2013b and authors' unpublished data.

claims.claim: Asymmetric BMP signaling plays an instructive role in the regulation of ISC self-renewal.
claims.source: To determine whether asymmetric BMP signaling plays an instructive role in the regulation of ISC self-renewal, we ectopically activated the pathway in precursor cells by expressing a constitutively active form of Tkv (TkvQ235D) (Nellen et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: Tested by gain-of-function experiments with TkvQ235D.

claims.claim: The employment of midgut epithelia as stem cell niche may provide a mechanism for direct communication between the niche and the environment.
claims.source: We speculate that the employment of midgut epithelia as stem cell niche may provide a mechanism for direct communication between the niche and the environment, allowing the production of niche signal and stem cell number to be regulated in response to various physiological and pathological stimuli.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of the biological significance of EC-derived niche signals.

claims.claim: Low levels of BMP pathway activity conferred by Sax-Put receptor complex appear to be enough to support ISC self-renewal.
claims.source: This result suggests that low levels of BMP pathway activity conferred by Sax-Put receptor complex appear to be enough to support ISC self-renewal (although not enough to prevent ISC from overproliferation).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that tkv8 single mutants retain ISCs.

claims.claim: Removal of either Dpp or Gbb resulted in ISC loss, implying that Dpp or Gbb homodimers failed to produce enough BMP activity to support ISC self-renewal.
claims.source: On the other hand, our results showed that removal of either Dpp or Gbb resulted in ISC loss, implying that Dpp or Gbb homodimers failed to produce enough BMP activity to support ISC self-renewal.
claims.evidence: Inferred from EC-specific Dpp or Gbb RNAi phenotypes.

claims.claim: Basal secretion coupled with BM trapping may establish a steep BMP activity gradient.
claims.source: Because type IV collagen/Vkg can physically interact with Dpp (Wang et al., 2008), we propose that basal secretion coupled with BM trapping may establish a steep BMP activity gradient so that basally localized ISC daughter cells receive higher levels of BMP than their more apically localized siblings, resulting in differential BMP signaling (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: Model proposed based on Dpp-GFP localization and vkg mutant phenotypes; cited from Wang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: BMP promotes ISC fate by inhibiting N pathway activity.
claims.source: Although it is possible that BMP and N pathways could act in parallel and exert opposing influence on ISC/EB fate choice, we favor a model in which BMP promotes ISC fate by inhibiting N pathway activity because loss of BMP signaling in precursor cells resulted in the ectopic expression of Su(H)-lacZ, which is a N pathway activity reporter, whereas gain of BMP signaling suppressed the expression of Su(H)-lacZ in precursor cells (Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis and marker expression analysis.

claims.claim: Differential BMP signaling sets up a difference in the levels of N signaling activity between the two daughter cells after an ISC division.
claims.source: Therefore, we propose that differential BMP signaling sets up a difference in the levels of N signaling activity between the two daughter cells after an ISC division.
claims.evidence: Model proposed based on asymmetric BMP signaling and epistasis with Notch.

claims.claim: The initial small difference in N pathway activity between apical and basal ISC daughter cells is amplified by N feedback regulation.
claims.source: The initial small difference in the N pathway activity between the apical and basal ISC daughter cells is amplified by N feedback regulation (Figure 9; Axelrod, 2010): N signaling in the apical cell inhibits Dl expression and Dl accumulation in the basal cell further strengthens N signaling in its apical sibling.
claims.evidence: Model incorporating known Notch-Delta feedback; cited from Axelrod, 2010.

claims.claim: Elevated N pathway activity in the apical ISC daughter cell may attenuate BMP signaling in this cell, forming another feedback mechanism to reinforce EB fate choice.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we also found that excessive N signaling could block BMP pathway activity, as indicated by the blockage of pMad staining in precursor cells expressing NICD (Figure 5M). We speculate that elevated N pathway activity in the apical ISC daughter cell may attenuate BMP signaling in this cell, forming another feedback mechanism to reinforce EB fate choice.
claims.evidence: Speculative model based on observation that NICD reduces pMad.

claims.claim: Asymmetric segregation of aPKC may dampen BMP signaling response in the apically localized ISC daughter cells.
claims.source: A recent study revealed that aPKC is asymmetrically inherited by apically localized ISC daughter cells and that aPKC promotes N pathway activity (Goulas et al., 2012). Therefore, asymmetric segregation of aPKC may dampen BMP signaling response in the apically localized ISC daughter cells, which could contribute to the differential BMP signaling.
claims.evidence: Speculative integration of aPKC asymmetry with BMP signaling; cited from Goulas et al., 2012.

results.result: BMP signaling is required for damage-induced ISC proliferation and epithelial regeneration. Knockdown of either type I (Tkv) or type II (Put) BMP receptors in precursor cells blocked DSS- or bleomycin-induced ISC proliferation and prevented the formation of differentiated enterocytes (ECs) and enteroendocrine cells (EEs).
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C7 are supported by quantitative data showing significant reduction in PH3+ mitotic cells (Figure 1B) and absence of differentiated GFP+ ECs/EEs in BMP receptor knockdown guts (Figure 1F-K, O-T). The experimental design includes appropriate controls and multiple damage-inducing agents.

results.result: Loss of BMP signaling causes ISC loss through altered cell fate determination rather than apoptosis. BMP receptor knockdown resulted in dramatic reduction of Dl+ ISCs and increase in Su(H)-lacZ+ EBs, with most precursor pairs containing two EBs instead of one ISC and one EB. This phenotype could not be rescued by blocking apoptosis, and twin-spot analysis confirmed a shift from asymmetric (82% ISC/EB) to symmetric non-self-renewing divisions (80% EB/EB).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are well-supported by quantitative immunostaining data (Figure 2A-G), twin-spot lineage tracing experiments (Figure 2K-M), and apoptosis rescue experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches provides strong evidence for the cell fate determination mechanism.

results.result: MARCM clonal analysis of putP null mutants confirms BMP requirement for ISC self-renewal and proper lineage differentiation. At 5 days after clone induction, 82% of putP clones contained two Su(H)-lacZ+ cells compared to 91% ISC/EB pairs in controls. At 12 days, putP clones lacked Pdm1+ ECs, but these appeared by 18 days, indicating delayed differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 are supported by quantitative MARCM clonal analysis at multiple time points (Figure 3A-K). The temporal progression from early cell fate defects to delayed differentiation is well-documented. However, the interpretation of delayed Pdm1 expression (C16) as a differentiation defect is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Tkv and Sax function redundantly in ISC self-renewal, and different degrees of BMP pathway inactivation produce distinct phenotypes. tkv8 single mutant clones overproliferated and retained ISCs, but combined loss of Tkv and Sax (either through tkv8 + Sax-RNAi or through Tkv-RNAi105834 targeting both receptors) resulted in ISC loss similar to putP mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are supported by systematic genetic analysis using multiple RNAi lines and mutant alleles (Figure 3L-T, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The molecular characterization of RNAi target sequences (C21) provides mechanistic insight. The dose-dependent phenotype model (C23) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: mad1-2 hypomorphic mutants phenocopy tkv8, and double mutants reveal non-cell-autonomous effects mediated by ECs. mad1-2 and tkv8 single mutant clones overproliferated and stimulated neighboring wild-type ISC proliferation, but tkv8 mad1-2 double mutants showed ISC loss without non-cell-autonomous effects. EC-specific BMP knockdown also stimulated ISC proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by clonal analysis with PH3 staining (Figure 3P-U, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and EC-specific RNAi experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The interpretation that non-cell-autonomous effects are mediated by ECs (C28) is well-supported by the correlation between EC presence and proliferation effects.

results.result: BMP signaling is asymmetrically activated in ISC/EB pairs. ISCs (Dl-lacZ+) show high pMad levels while EBs (Su(H)>GFP+) show low pMad levels. The BMP target gene dad-lacZ is similarly enriched in ISCs. During mitosis, pMad is evenly distributed, suggesting asymmetry arises post-division. A small fraction (8%) of divisions produce symmetric ISC/ISC pairs with equally high pMad.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are supported by immunostaining data showing differential pMad and dad-lacZ expression (Figure 4A-F'). The observation of equal pMad distribution during mitosis (C31) is important for mechanistic understanding. Sample sizes are adequate for the symmetric division frequency (C32).

results.result: Ectopic BMP signaling promotes ISC self-renewal and symmetric self-renewing divisions. Expression of constitutively active TkvQ235D or coexpression of Dpp and Gbb resulted in formation of large ISC-like cell clusters. Twin-spot analysis showed TkvQ235D increased symmetric ISC/ISC divisions from 9% to 77%. Dpp and Gbb act synergistically, likely as heterodimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are strongly supported by gain-of-function experiments with quantitative twin-spot analysis (Figure 4H-S). The synergistic effect of Dpp+Gbb versus individual ligands (C37) supports the heterodimer model (C38), though the heterodimer formation is inferred rather than directly demonstrated here.

results.result: BMP signaling promotes ISC self-renewal by antagonizing Notch-mediated differentiation. Notch activation (NICD) completely suppressed BMP-induced ISC clusters, while Notch loss rescued Dl+ cells in BMP-deficient backgrounds. ISC-like cells in N-RNAi guts showed low pMad levels, and NICD expression reduced pMad staining, suggesting Notch acts downstream of or parallel to BMP.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by comprehensive epistasis experiments (Figure 5). The genetic interactions clearly demonstrate that Notch acts downstream of BMP in this context. The observation that BMP is still required for proliferation of N-deficient ISCs (C43) adds nuance to the model.

results.result: Dpp and Gbb are expressed in enterocytes (ECs) with complementary regional patterns. dpp-Gal4 drives GFP expression in ECs along the A-P axis with high expression in posterior, middle, and anterior regions. RNA in situ hybridization confirmed dpp and gbb mRNA in ECs but not in precursor cells or visceral muscle. High gbb expression correlates with low dpp expression regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by multiple complementary approaches including Gal4 reporter expression (Figure 6A-D') and RNA in situ hybridization (Figure 6E-F', supplementary figures). The absence of expression in precursor cells and VM is clearly documented. The complementary expression patterns suggest coordinated regulation.

results.result: EC-derived Dpp and Gbb are the major source of BMP signals for ISC self-renewal. EC-specific overexpression of Dpp+Gbb increased Dl+ cells, while strong RNAi knockdown of either Dpp or Gbb in ECs caused ISC loss, reduced pMad signaling, and impaired injury response. Combined weak RNAi also caused ISC loss. In contrast, tracheal or VM-specific Dpp knockdown had no significant effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 are supported by extensive tissue-specific manipulation experiments (Figure 7, supplementary figures). The use of strong and weak RNAi lines (C51, C54) demonstrates dose-dependency. RT-qPCR validation of knockdown efficiency strengthens the conclusions. The contrast with tracheal/VM knockdown (C55-C57) is compelling evidence for EC as the primary source.

results.result: Dpp is basally enriched and can redistribute Gbb. When expressed in ECs, Dpp-GFP was enriched on the basal side of epithelia and colocalized with basal Golgi markers, suggesting preferential basal secretion. Gbb-GFP was initially uniform but became basally enriched when coexpressed with Dpp. Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed Dpp-Gbb physical interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by localization studies (Figure 8A-C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and biochemical co-IP experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The Golgi colocalization (C60) supports but does not definitively prove basal secretion. The Dpp-Gbb interaction provides a mechanism for the redistribution effect.

results.result: Type IV collagen/Viking regulates ISC self-renewal by restricting BMP signaling distribution. vkg mutant midguts showed excessive Dl+ cells, reduced Su(H)-lacZ+ cells, and clusters of precursor cells with high pMad. Reducing Dpp dosage suppressed the vkg phenotype. vkg mutants retained less Dpp-GFP at the basement membrane, suggesting Vkg traps BMP ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by vkg mutant analysis with multiple readouts (Figure 8F-Q, supplementary figures). The genetic interaction with dpp (C64) provides strong support for the model. The reduced Dpp-GFP retention at BM in vkg mutants (C65) directly supports the trapping mechanism, though quantification could be more robust.

results.result: Prior studies established multiple roles for BMP signaling in midgut homeostasis, including copper cell differentiation and ISC proliferation regulation. Peak BMP signaling in the middle region specifies copper cells, and reduction in BMP activity causes ISC overproliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are appropriately cited from recent literature (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013a, 2013b; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004). These claims provide important context for the current work but are not original findings of this manuscript.

results.result: BMP signaling has non-cell-autonomous effects on ISC proliferation mediated through enterocytes. Both tkv8 and mad1-2 mutant clones caused excessive proliferation of neighboring wild-type ISCs, and EC-specific BMP inactivation stimulated ISC proliferation by inducing JAK-STAT and EGFR pathway ligands.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by clonal analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C) and EC-specific knockdown experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-E). The mechanism involving JAK-STAT and EGFR ligands (C70) is partially supported by citation and authors' unpublished data, requiring future validation.

results.result: The authors tested whether asymmetric BMP signaling plays an instructive role in ISC self-renewal using gain-of-function approaches with constitutively active Tkv.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 accurately describes the experimental rationale. The gain-of-function experiments with TkvQ235D (covered in other results) directly address this question and support an instructive role for BMP signaling.

results.result: The authors speculate that using midgut epithelia as stem cell niche may enable direct communication between the niche and environment, allowing dynamic regulation of niche signals and stem cell numbers in response to physiological and pathological stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is explicitly speculative and not directly tested in this study. While the EC-derived niche signal model is well-supported, the proposed advantage for environmental responsiveness remains a hypothesis requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: The authors propose that low BMP activity via Sax-Put is sufficient for ISC self-renewal (though not to prevent overproliferation), while Dpp or Gbb homodimers cannot provide sufficient activity. This is inferred from tkv8 single mutants retaining ISCs while EC-specific Dpp or Gbb knockdown causes ISC loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are reasonable inferences from the genetic data, but the mechanistic explanation remains speculative. Alternative explanations (ligand concentration, competition, stability) are discussed but not definitively tested. The model requires biochemical validation of receptor-ligand interactions and signaling thresholds.

results.result: The authors propose a model where basal secretion of Dpp coupled with basement membrane trapping by type IV collagen/Vkg establishes a steep BMP activity gradient, resulting in higher BMP signaling in basally localized ISC daughters compared to apical daughters.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 integrates multiple experimental observations (Dpp-GFP basal enrichment, Vkg-Dpp interaction from Wang et al. 2008, vkg mutant phenotypes) into a coherent model. While the gradient itself is not directly visualized, the supporting evidence is strong. The model is testable and consistent with all presented data.

results.result: The authors propose a model where BMP inhibits Notch pathway activity to promote ISC fate, with differential BMP signaling establishing differences in Notch activity between daughter cells. This initial difference is amplified by Notch-Delta feedback regulation, where Notch signaling in the apical cell inhibits Dl expression while Dl accumulation in the basal cell strengthens Notch in the apical sibling.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 synthesize the epistasis data and known Notch-Delta feedback mechanisms (cited from Axelrod, 2010) into a coherent model. The model is well-supported by the genetic data showing BMP antagonizes Notch (C39-C42) and by the observation of asymmetric BMP signaling (C29-C33). The feedback amplification is based on established Notch biology.

results.result: The authors speculate that elevated Notch activity in the apical ISC daughter may attenuate BMP signaling, forming a feedback mechanism to reinforce EB fate choice. This is based on the observation that NICD expression reduces pMad staining.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is explicitly speculative and based on a single observation (Figure 5M) showing NICD reduces pMad. While intriguing, this potential feedback mechanism requires further validation including dose-response analysis, temporal dynamics, and identification of molecular mediators. The physiological relevance is unclear.

results.result: The authors speculate that asymmetric segregation of aPKC to apical ISC daughters may dampen BMP signaling response in these cells, contributing to differential BMP signaling. This integrates a recent finding (Goulas et al., 2012) that aPKC is asymmetrically inherited and promotes Notch activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is speculative and attempts to integrate aPKC asymmetry with the BMP signaling model. While aPKC's role in promoting Notch is established (cited), the proposed effect on BMP signaling is not tested. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a supported conclusion.
